description: Team of 4 Of highly skilled individuals , 2 coders, 1 Artist and 1 Analyst.
summary:
NINTH is a public astronomy website and blink comparator based on actual NASA SPHEREx observations of the M101 field. It lets people compare eight images from different times, switch between views, explore changes in wavelengths and spot objects that might have moved. 
The project addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by converting a professional search technique into a public-friendly tool. It also helps users understand how motion can reveal distant solar-system objects and also clarifies the limits of the data. 
It's important to note that NINTH does not announce a Planet Nine discovery. Instead, it shows people a transparent way to check out real observations and see how scientific evidence gets tested.
details:
NINTH loads eight SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive. Users can select any two dates, blink between them, drag a comparison seam, view a difference map, and inspect the wavelength at any point in the image. They can also record field marks and export them as JSON for later review.

The project was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, supported by Python scripts for querying archive data, processing FITS files, handling WCS information, reprojecting images, and generating comparison assets. It runs in a standard web browser and does not require special hardware.

The creative focus was making a technical astronomy workflow feel understandable and engaging without overstating the results. The team considered accessibility, clear instructions, scientific honesty, responsive design, visual storytelling, image noise, detector differences, wavelength variation, and traceable data sources. The intended impact is to help more people experience how astronomers investigate possible moving objects and why repeated observations are necessary before calling something a discovery.
